label: Willmore Surfaces
notes: Open by making the variational question concrete. The chapter asks which surfaces make bending energy stationary after the topological part has been separated away. The notebook treats the Willmore functional as a geometric diagnostic that can be sampled, transformed, and checked.

label: Three Curvature-Squared Energies
notes: Use this slide to sort the energy vocabulary before doing any variation. Mean curvature, the trace-free part, and the full second fundamental form carry different pointwise information, but on a closed surface their integrals differ by a Gauss-Bonnet term.

label: Gauss-Bonnet Removes The Offset
notes: Emphasize that the offset is topological, not numerical noise. Once the Euler characteristic is fixed, minimizing one curvature-squared package is equivalent to minimizing another package shifted by a constant. This is why the notebook compares energies through invariant differences.

label: Willmore Density
notes: This is the pointwise object to watch in computations. A surface patch contributes area times squared mean curvature, so a small region with large bending can dominate the visual heat map even when the patch is tiny.

label: The Euler-Lagrange Residual
notes: Present the equation as a residual, not as a formula to memorize. A Willmore surface balances the Laplacian of mean curvature against cubic curvature terms. In a numerical lab, the residual tells the learner where the surface still wants to move.

label: Elastic Cylinders
notes: Connect back to the earlier curve chapters. A cylinder built over a planar curve converts the surface equation into a curve equation, so the same elastic intuition reappears with a surface area factor attached. This is the bridge that lets learners reuse their curvature-energy instincts before facing fully two-dimensional variations.

label: Inversion Test
notes: Use inversion as the main conceptual surprise. The surface may look radically different after inversion, but the conformal density carries the same Willmore information away from singular points. The learner should track energy rather than visual size.

label: Sphere And Torus Benchmarks
notes: Benchmarks keep the lecture honest. The round sphere is the reference equality case, while tori make the dependence on the radius ratio visible. The notebook uses parameter sweeps so the minimum is a feature the learner can inspect.

label: Proof Scaffold
notes: The proof route has three rungs: vary the area element, vary the curvature, then integrate by parts until the normal speed is arbitrary. Stress that boundary terms vanish only under the closed-surface or compact-support assumptions.

label: Applied Lab
notes: Frame the lab as a design loop. Choose a one-parameter family, compute energy and residual, and decide whether the parameter is moving toward or away from Willmore balance. The important habit is to pair every heat map with an invariant number.

label: Diagnostics
notes: Close the technical part with checks. Area elements should stay positive, the Gauss-Bonnet estimate should match the topology, inversion comparisons should agree within tolerance, and residual plots should identify the same regions highlighted by curvature.

label: Takeaways
notes: End by connecting the chapter to the course arc. Elastic curves taught bending as a variational signal; Willmore surfaces are the surface analogue, strengthened by topology, conformal invariance, and computational diagnostics. Ask learners to leave with one habit: every beautiful surface picture needs an invariant and a residual check.
